q: A student sorts buttons into a big group and a small group. What property is used?
e: Big and small tell the size of the buttons.

q: Which object is HEAVIER than a feather?
e: A rock has more weight than a feather.

q: Objects are sorted into two groups: SMOOTH and BUMPY. Which property is used?
e: Smooth and bumpy tell how objects feel.

q: Which object is the LIGHTEST?
e: A feather weighs the least of these objects.

q: Which group has objects that all have the same SHAPE?
o: a ball, a globe, an orange
a book, a can, a ball
a drum, a die, a marble
a ball, a box, a cone
e: A ball, a globe, and an orange are all round like spheres.

q: A student puts a red crayon, a red apple, and a red hat in one group. How were they sorted?
e: All three objects are red.

q: Which object is LARGER than a marble but SMALLER than a basketball?
e: A baseball is bigger than a marble and smaller than a basketball.

q: What happens to an ice cube left in a warm room?
e: Heat makes ice melt into water.

q: What happens to water placed in a freezer?
e: Cooling makes water freeze into ice.

q: A chocolate bar sits in a hot car. What will happen?
o: it will turn into a rock
e: Heat makes chocolate melt.

q: A puddle of water is left in the cold on a winter night. What may happen?
e: Cold air can freeze water.

q: What happens to butter in a hot pan?
e: Heat makes butter melt.

q: A popsicle drips on a sunny day. What caused the drips?
e: Heat from the Sun melts the popsicle.

q: Which object will stay a solid in a hot room for a long time?
e: A metal spoon does not melt in an ordinary hot room.

q: A toy car has wheels, a body, and an axle. What are these?
e: The wheels, body, and axle are parts that make up the toy.

q: A student takes a toy apart and puts it back together. What does this show?
o: an object is made of parts
e: A whole object is made of organized parts.

q: A bicycle needs wheels, pedals, and a frame to work. What is a bicycle?
o: a system of parts working together
e: A bike works because its parts work together as a system.

q: A flashlight has a case, a bulb, and batteries. What happens if the batteries are missing?
o: it will turn into a lamp
e: Each part is needed for the whole flashlight to work.

q: Which is a part of a chair?
e: A chair has legs, a seat, and a back.

q: A puzzle is made of many pieces. What happens if one piece is lost?
o: the whole puzzle is not complete
e: A whole system needs all of its parts.

q: A wagon has a handle, a body, and wheels. Which part helps it roll?
e: Wheels let the wagon roll.

q: A student kicks a ball. What force starts the ball moving?
e: A kick pushes the ball so it starts to move.

q: A student opens a drawer by taking the handle and bringing it toward them. What force is this?
e: Moving the handle toward you is a pull.

q: A goalie catches a rolling ball. What did the goalie do to the ball?
e: The goalie's hands stopped the ball's motion.

q: A student hits a rolling ball with a bat and it moves the other way. What changed?
e: The hit made the ball go a different direction.

q: Which makes a swing go higher?
e: A bigger push makes the swing move faster and higher.

q: A cart is pushed gently, then pushed harder. What happens to the cart?
e: A harder push makes the cart move faster.

q: A student pulls a wagon forward. Which tells how the wagon's motion changed?
e: A pull started the wagon moving.

q: A student predicts a ball will roll farther when pushed harder. What does the student need to test?
o: push the ball softly and then hard
e: To test the prediction, change only the strength of the push.

q: A toy car rolls down a steep ramp and a low ramp. Which ramp makes the car go faster?
e: A steeper ramp makes the car go faster.

q: A student wants to see if a heavier ball needs a bigger push. What should the student compare?
o: a light ball and a heavy ball
two balls of the same weight
e: Comparing a light ball with a heavy ball tests the idea.

q: A student pushes a toy car on a rug and on a smooth floor. On which does the car most likely go farther?
e: A smooth floor lets objects roll farther than a rug.

q: Before pushing a box, a student says, 'I think it will slide.' What is this?
e: A prediction tells what you think will happen.

q: A student records how far a car rolls after a soft push and a hard push. What is being measured?
e: The distance traveled shows the effect of the push.

q: A student pushes the same car with two different pushes. Which should stay the SAME to keep the test fair?
e: Only the push should change. The car and the floor stay the same.

q: Which uses heat?
e: A stove gives heat to cook food.

q: A clothes dryer uses heat to do what?
e: Heat in a dryer removes water from clothes.

q: Which tool gives heat to a home in winter?
e: A heater warms the air in a home.

q: A toaster turns bread into toast. What does a toaster give to the bread?
e: A toaster heats the bread.

q: Which is a source of heat for cooking?
e: An oven makes heat that cooks food.

q: Which job uses heat from the Sun?
e: The Sun's heat dries wet clothes on a line.

q: A student wraps up in a blanket. How does the blanket help?
e: A blanket holds in the heat from the body.

q: Which change can be turned back to what it was?
e: Water can be frozen again to make ice.

q: Which change can NOT be turned back?
e: Once a cake is baked, it cannot be turned back into batter.

q: Melted butter is placed in the refrigerator. What happens?
e: Cooling melted butter makes it solid again.

q: A student cooks an egg. Can the egg be changed back to a raw egg?
o: no, cooking changes it for good
e: Cooking an egg is a change that cannot be reversed.

q: Which is a change that CAN be reversed?
o: melting chocolate and letting it cool
e: Melted chocolate becomes solid when it cools.

q: A wax crayon melts in the sun. What can a student do to make it hard again?
e: Cooling makes melted wax harden again.

q: Which two changes both CANNOT be reversed?
o: baking bread and cooking an egg
e: Baking and cooking make new materials that cannot be changed back.

q: How many seasons are in a year?
e: The four seasons are spring, summer, fall, and winter.

q: Which season comes after winter?
e: The order is spring, summer, fall, then winter.

q: Which season comes after summer?
e: Fall comes after summer.

q: Flowers bloom and baby animals are born. Which season is it?
e: Many plants and animals begin growing in spring.

q: Which list shows the seasons in order, starting with spring?
e: The seasons repeat in the same order each year.

q: Many trees lose their leaves. What happens to the days soon after?
e: After fall comes winter, when days are colder.

q: It is winter now. What will the next season be?
e: After winter, spring comes.

q: Which soil has tiny, loose grains that feel gritty?
e: Sand has gritty grains that do not stick together.

q: Which soil feels sticky when wet and can be shaped?
e: Clay feels sticky when wet and holds a shape.

q: Which soil is dark and has bits of dead plants?
e: Topsoil is dark and has bits of dead plants that help plants grow.

q: A student looks at soil with a hand lens. What can the student observe?
e: A hand lens helps show small particles in soil.

q: Which soil is best for growing most plants?
e: Topsoil has nutrients that plants need.

q: A student rubs two soils between her fingers. One feels gritty and one feels smooth and sticky. Which has the larger particles?
e: Sand is gritty and has larger particles than clay.

q: A student sorts soil into groups by color and texture. What is the student doing?
e: Sorting by properties is classifying.

q: What can rain do to loose soil on a hill?
e: Moving water can wash soil downhill.

q: A stream carries sand and pebbles downstream. What is the water doing?
e: Flowing water moves particles from one place to another.

q: After a heavy rain, muddy water runs down a slope. What does the mud show?
e: Muddy water has soil moved by the rain.

q: Where do rocks and sand end up when a river slows down?
o: they are dropped on the bottom
e: A slow river drops what it carries.

q: Pouring water on a pile of sand makes the sand do what?
e: Water moves sand from where it was.

q: How could a student show that water moves soil?
o: pour water on a pile of soil on a tray
e: Pouring water on soil shows how water moves particles.

q: Which change is MOST likely after a flood?
o: soil and rocks are moved to new places
e: Floodwater carries soil and rocks to new places.

q: Which body of water is the biggest?
e: Oceans cover most of Earth and are the biggest.

q: Which body of water is usually saltwater?
e: Ocean water is salty.

q: Which is a small, shallow pool of water left after it rains?
e: A puddle is a small pool after rain.

q: Which body of water flows in a long line to a larger body of water?
e: A river flows across land toward another body of water.

q: Which is larger?
e: A lake is larger than a puddle, a pond, or a stream.

q: A student finds water that is freshwater and very small, with plants growing in it. Which is it most likely?
e: A pond is a small body of freshwater.

q: Which two bodies of water are both freshwater?
e: Lakes and streams are usually freshwater. Oceans are saltwater.

q: What can you wear on a rainy day?
e: A raincoat keeps you dry.

q: Which weather word means the sky has many clouds?
e: Cloudy means many clouds cover the sky.

q: A student sees a flag flapping hard. What does this show about the weather?
e: A flapping flag shows strong wind.

q: The ground is icy. Which choice is best?
e: Icy ground is slippery, so boots and careful steps help.

q: Which weather is hot?
o: a summer afternoon in the sun
e: Hot weather happens on a sunny summer afternoon.

q: Which tool tells how hot or cold it is?
e: A thermometer measures temperature.

q: A student plans a picnic. The weather report says rain all day. What is the best choice?
e: Weather affects what people decide to do.

q: How do plants use water?
o: they take it in through their roots
they drink it with a straw
e: Plants take in water through their roots.

q: How do many animals use soil?
e: Some animals dig burrows in soil.

q: How do people use rocks?
e: People use rocks and stone for building.

q: How do animals use water?
e: Animals need to drink water.

q: A bird drinks from a stream. What does the bird use?
e: The bird gets a drink from the water.

q: Ants live under the ground. What do they use for their homes?
e: Ants dig tunnels in soil.

q: Which uses rock, soil, and water together?
o: a garden with a stone path
e: A garden uses soil and water, and a stone path uses rock.

q: Why is it important to save water?
o: there is only so much fresh water
e: Fresh water is limited, so we should use it carefully.

q: What happens if people waste water?
o: there may not be enough later
e: Wasting water can leave less for later.

q: Who needs clean water?
e: All living things need water.

q: Which shows a good reason to conserve water?
o: so there is enough for everyone
e: Saving water helps make sure everyone has enough.

q: A city has a dry summer. Why should people use less water?
o: water in lakes and rivers may run low
e: A dry summer can lower water supplies.

q: Which sentence about clean water is true?
o: clean water is needed to stay healthy
e: People need clean water to drink and stay healthy.

q: What does conserve mean?
e: To conserve means to save and use carefully.

q: Which action saves water?
o: fill the sink and let it overflow
play in the sprinkler all day
turn off the faucet while brushing your teeth
e: Turning off the faucet stops water from being wasted.

q: Which action keeps a pond clean?
o: put trash in a trash can
e: Keeping trash out of water protects it.

q: Which is a way to use less water?
o: let a hose run all day
e: A short shower uses less water.

q: A faucet is dripping. What should be done?
o: tell a grown-up so it can be fixed
collect the drips and spill them out
e: A dripping faucet wastes water until it is fixed.

q: What should you do with litter near a stream?
o: pick it up and throw it in a trash can
e: Litter near a stream can wash in, so it should be put in a trash can.

q: Which is the best way to water a garden without wasting water?
o: leave the hose on all night
water at noon in the heat
e: Watering in the morning means less water dries up.

q: Which action protects lakes and rivers?
o: keeping chemicals and trash out of the water
e: Clean water stays clean when pollution is kept out.

q: Which is a living thing?
e: A tree needs water and food, grows, and makes new trees.

q: Which is nonliving?
e: A rock does not eat, grow, or have young.

q: Which needs food, water, and air to live?
e: A puppy is a living thing that has basic needs.

q: A butterfly lays eggs. What does this show?
e: Living things make young.

q: Which does NOT grow or make young?
e: A toy robot is nonliving.

q: Which list has only living things?
o: a tree, a book, a bird
a rock, a ball, a tree
a frog, a tree, a bird
a frog, a rock, a bird
e: A frog, a tree, and a bird are all living.

q: A student sees a seed. Is it living?
o: yes, it can grow into a plant
e: A seed is alive and can grow into a plant.

q: A terrarium has plants, soil, and a lid. Which is nonliving?
e: Soil is a nonliving part of a terrarium.

q: In an aquarium, fish need water. What does this show?
o: living things depend on nonliving things
e: Fish depend on water, which is nonliving.

q: A plant in a terrarium gets light through the glass. What does the plant need the light for?
e: Plants use light to make food.

q: Which is a living thing in an aquarium?
e: A snail is alive. Gravel, water, and a plastic castle are not.

q: A student sprays a terrarium with water. Why?
e: Plants need water to live.

q: In a classroom aquarium, what happens if the water gets very dirty?
e: Living things need clean water.

q: Which pair shows a living thing depending on a nonliving thing?
e: The fish needs water, a nonliving thing.

q: What do most plants use to make their own food?
e: Plants use light from the Sun to make food.

q: A rabbit eats grass. What does the rabbit get from the grass?
e: The rabbit gets energy from eating the grass.

q: A hawk eats a mouse and a mouse eats seeds. Which shows the food chain in order?
e: The arrows point to what eats the food: seed to mouse to hawk.

q: Which animal eats other animals?
e: A hawk eats mice and other small animals.

q: Which is the first link in most food chains?
e: Plants make food, so most food chains start with a plant.

q: A frog eats a fly. What would happen to the frog if there were no flies?
e: Animals depend on what they eat.

q: A cricket eats plants. A bird eats the cricket. Which does the bird depend on for food?
e: The bird gets its food from the cricket, which is a small insect.

q: A bird has wings. What can wings help many birds do?
e: Wings help most birds fly.

q: A fish has fins and gills. What do fins help it do?
e: Fins help fish move in water.

q: Which animal has fur that keeps it warm?
e: Fur keeps a bear warm.

q: A duck has webbed feet. What do they help it do?
e: Webbed feet push water to help a duck swim.

q: A turtle has a hard shell. What does the shell help it do?
e: A shell protects a turtle.

q: Which animal has a long neck that helps it reach leaves in tall trees?
e: A giraffe's long neck helps it reach high leaves.

q: Why does a woodpecker have a strong, pointed beak?
o: to peck into trees for food
to make a nest of mud
e: A woodpecker's beak is used to peck wood for insects.

q: A bird starts its life inside what?
e: Birds hatch from eggs.

q: Which order shows a bird's life cycle?
e: A bird hatches from an egg as a chick, then grows into an adult.

q: Which is a mammal?
e: A dog is a mammal.

q: How do baby mammals get their first food?
o: they drink milk from their mother
e: Mammal mothers feed their babies milk.

q: A fish starts as an egg and hatches into a tiny fish. What comes next?
o: it grows into an adult fish
e: A young fish grows into an adult fish.

q: A puppy grows up to be what?
e: A puppy grows into an adult dog.

q: Which animal does NOT start life inside an egg?
e: A horse is a mammal and the baby grows inside the mother.

q: A kitten looks most like which animal?
e: Young animals look like their parents.

q: A baby duck has feathers, a beak, and webbed feet like its parents. What does this show?
o: young animals look like their parents
e: Young animals resemble their parents.

q: A calf is a young cow. What does the calf have like its parents?
e: A calf looks like a small cow.

q: A puppy has ears and a tail like its mother. Which is the same?
e: The puppy has the same kinds of body parts as its mother.

q: A chick looks small. How is it like its parents?
o: it has feathers and a beak
e: A chick has feathers and a beak like adult chickens.

q: A baby giraffe looks like which animal?
e: A baby giraffe looks like an adult giraffe.

q: A student finds a baby animal with spots. The mother also has spots. What can the student say?
o: young animals never look like parents
young animals can look like their parents
e: The baby and mother share the same pattern.
